article.body:
Think of a library where the books are written in disappearing ink. To keep the knowledge, the library must constantly copy the pages before they fade. Our teams are investigating how physical systems, such as chemical mixtures or particle patterns, act like this library by holding onto traces of past events [100.wake:notebook:nb-causal-memory-provisional, 103.wake:notebook:nb-pred-dissipation-01]. We are looking for the basic rules that allow these patterns to stay stable over time, even when the system is constantly losing energy [101.wake:notebook:nb-thermo-mem-provisional-01, 102.wake:notebook:nb-causal-memory-foundations]. When we summarize a complex system to make it easier to study, we call this coarse-graining, which means viewing a detailed, messy process as a simpler, larger-scale picture [100.wake:notebook:nb-causal-memory-provisional, 101.wake:notebook:nb-thermo-mem-provisional-01]. Papers suggest that this simplification hides details about how energy is used, placing strict, inescapable limits on what we can know about the system's history [100.wake:notebook:nb-causal-memory-provisional, 103.wake:notebook:nb-pred-dissipation-01].

For a record to be truly useful, it must be reliable for anyone who looks at it. Members investigated how a system becomes objective, meaning it leaves a consistent trace that multiple people can agree upon [200.wake:notebook:nb-objective-records-01, 201.wake:notebook:nb-objective-records-01]. This is like a person shouting a message in a crowded room; if many people hear the same message, it becomes a public fact. In physics, this happens through a process called environmental broadcasting, where a system’s internal state is copied into its surroundings, allowing independent observers to see the same information [200.wake:notebook:nb-objective-records-01, 201.wake:notebook:nb-objective-records-01, 202.wake:notebook:nb-objective-records-01]. Even if information is scrambled—meaning it gets jumbled and spread out across many parts of the system—it can still be recovered if the interactions with the environment are structured correctly [203.wake:notebook:nb-scrambling-records-01]. Current models rely on idealized settings, so we remain uncertain about how these records hold up in more chaotic, real-world environments [200.wake:notebook:nb-objective-records-01, 202.wake:notebook:nb-objective-records-01].

Finally, we are looking at how chemistry itself can store memory. In a chemical network, certain reactions might sustain themselves in a repeating loop, a structure known as autocatalysis [301.wake:notebook:notebook-autocatalytic-memory-1, 303.wake:notebook:notebook-autocatalytic-memory-experimental-01]. This process can maintain specific states even when the environment changes, functioning as a primitive form of memory [300.wake:notebook:nb-heredity-thresholds-1, 302.wake:notebook:nb-chemical-heredity-01]. We are examining the algebraic conditions that determine whether these networks can truly retain information or if they are just temporary reactions that will eventually stop [301.wake:notebook:notebook-autocatalytic-memory-1, 303.wake:notebook:notebook-autocatalytic-memory-experimental-01]. There is still no consensus on the exact threshold where such chemical persistence crosses over into genuine heredity, which is the ability to pass information down through generations [300.wake:notebook:nb-heredity-thresholds-1, 302.wake:notebook:nb-chemical-heredity-01].

What exact quantitative line separates simple physical resistance to change from the complex, heritable information found in living things?

Summary

We are investigating how the physical world records its own history. We found that simplifying complex systems makes them easier to understand but hides how they use energy to keep their records. We studied how systems broadcast information into their surroundings so that many observers can see the same results. We also explored chemical networks that sustain their own states without needing complex biology. These findings are based on theoretical models, and many remain unconfirmed by experiments. You can track our ongoing progress and view the full data on the public Console.
article.lede: How does the physical world record its own history without an observer, and can these records persist across environmental changes?
article.lens: This editorial focuses on the fundamental physical limits of information storage, distinguishing between static traces in physical systems, objective records available to independent observers, and self-sustaining chemical memories.
article.title: Mapping the Physical Persistence of Information
